subject: Critical Thinking
title: Thinking in Scenarios: Plan for Multiple Futures
description: A fast breakdown of Thinking in Scenarios: Plan for Multiple Futures for builders.

hook.text: Shell Oil survived the 1973 oil crisis because they'd already imagined it. While competitors panicked, Shell adapted.

buildup.text: Scenario planning: instead of predicting one future, imagine 3-4 plausible futures and prepare for all of them.

discovery.text: It was developed at RAND Corporation and Shell in the 1960s-70s. Military strategists still use it for war planning.

twist.text: The point isn't to predict which scenario will happen — it's to build strategies that work across multiple scenarios.

climax.text: Robust strategies beat optimal ones. Optimizing for one future is fragile. Preparing for many is resilient.

punchline.text: Don't predict the future. Prepare for several of them.

quiz.question: What is the goal of scenario planning?
options: Build strategies that work across multiple plausible futures

details.summary: Scenario thinking develops multiple plausible futures rather than betting on a single prediction. By preparing for several possibilities simultaneously, you become robust to surprise instead of fragile to it.
details.whyItMatters: The future is inherently uncertain. Planning for one scenario creates fragility; planning for several creates resilience and adaptability.
takeaways: Shell Oil pioneered scenario planning and survived the 1973 oil crisis
Good scenarios are plausible, distinct, and challenging

faq.question: How many scenarios should you develop for effective planning?
faq.answer: Three to four is typical: an optimistic case, a pessimistic case, and one or two mid-range alternatives. Too few misses important possibilities; too many becomes unmanageable. Each scenario should tell a coherent story.

faq.question: How did scenario planning help Shell Oil survive the 1973 crisis?
faq.answer: Shell had already developed scenarios that included a dramatic oil price increase. When OPEC cut production, Shell was the only major oil company with contingency plans ready, giving them a massive competitive advantage.
